item.title: Ebola Virus VP40 C-terminal Lysine Residue Mediates Lipid Interactions and Dimer-Dimer Interactions.
item.author: Woods HM, Narkhede YB, Karki U, Norris MJ, Chapagain PP, Wiest O, Stahelin RV.
item.description:
The Ebola virus (EBOV) matrix protein VP40 is the main driver of viral assembly and budding, processes which depend on its ability to oligomerize at the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane (PM). VP40 forms dimers in the cytoplasm that traffic to the membrane and assemble into higher-order oligomers, but the specific molecular determinants governing the stability of these oligomeric interfaces are not fully understood. Here, we investigate the role of the C-terminal lysine residue, Lys 326 , in mediating VP40-lipid and VP40-VP40 interactions. Using a combination of molecular dynamics simulations and computational site-saturation mutagenesis, we predicted that while Lys 326 has a minimal role in the stability of the isolated VP40 dimer, it is a critical determinant in stabilizing the interfaces of higher-order structures like tetramers and hexamers. item.title: Dysfunction of three CD36 variants is due to impaired glycosylation and trafficking.
item.author: Tillison EA, Jovanovic V, Luu QQ, Chen Y, Sahoo D.
item.description:
CD36 deficiency is characterized by the loss of CD36 due to genetic mutations. Clinical studies have associated CD36 deficiency with hyperlipidemia, insulin resistance, and cardiomyopathy. However, the structural and functional effects of human CD36 variants remain poorly understood. P90S is a causative mutation of CD36 deficiency while E123K and S127L are of unknown significance and typically found in malarial endemic regions. Despite their variable phenotypes, they are all located in the same structural region of CD36. In this study, we expressed these three naturally occurring human CD36 variants in HEK293 cells and found that all variants exhibited impaired oxLDL binding and uptake that was associated with reduced expression, shortened half-lives, and altered glycan processing, consistent with defects in receptor maturation. item.title: Influence of hemin on biophysical properties of membranes.
item.author: Laspa Z, Jarnot N, Andronico L, Sych T, Rohlfing AK, Gone N, Castor T, Pillaiyar T, Laufer S, Sezgin E, Gawaz MP.
item.description:
Hemin released from erythrocytes activates platelets through both receptor-dependent and receptor-independent mechanisms. While lower hemin concentrations predominantly activate the immune receptor tyrosine-based activation motif (ITAM) signaling via glycoprotein VI (GPVI) and C-type lectin-like receptor 2 (CLEC-2), higher concentrations induce pronounced receptor-independent cellular alterations, including loss of mitochondrial membrane potential, generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), lipid peroxidation, and plasma membrane fragmentation. However, the mechanism of receptor-independent effect of hemin is still unclear. item.title: The expression of the collagen chaperone Hsp47 is regulated by mechanical loading through the YAP/TEAD pathway.
item.author: Kasai A, Ito S, Ushioda R, Nagata K.
item.description:
Mechanical stimuli maintain tissue structure by regulating extracellular matrix (ECM) composition. Collagen, a major ECM component, requires heat shock protein 47 (Hsp47), a collagen-specific molecular chaperone, for proper folding and maturation. However, the molecular pathways linking mechanical stress to collagen biosynthesis through the regulation of Hsp47 expression are not fully understood. In this study, we demonstrate that the Hippo signaling pathway, mediated by the YAP/TEAD complex, directly controls Hsp47 transcription in response to mechanical loading. In a tail suspension mouse model, mechanical unloading induced YAP degradation, resulting in reduced Hsp47 expression and impaired collagen quality. item.title: Glycoconjugate diversification in Campylobacter concisus is determined by two glycosyltransferases.
item.author: Knox HL, Arbour CA, Xia C, Costello CE, Imperiali B, Allen KN.
item.description:
Bacterial glycoconjugates are structurally diverse, with enormous variation in sugar identity, modifications and linkages. Glycoconjugates play key roles in numerous cell functions, acting as the primary interface with the environment. Asparagine (N)-linked glycosylation has been extensively studied in the pathogenic Campylobacter genus, due to the availability of numerous genome sequences and the highly conserved pathway logic, despite the final N-linked glycan product diversity. We recently reported on a partitioning of N-linked glycan structures between the Campylobacter species, focused on the inclusion of a C6-carboxyl-sugar in the third position of the growing glycan in Campylobacter concisus. item.title: Cooperative Repression of γ-Globin by LYAR and NONO.
item.author: Wu D, Shangguan W, Wang X, Liu T, Li W, Liao R, Meng X, Xing M, Zhu Y, Zhang R, Li F, Chen B, Huang DCS, Zhao Q.
item.description:
Developmental silencing of γ-globin is a central event in hemoglobin switching, and reactivation of γ-globin expression effectively alleviates the severity of β-thalassemia and sickle cell disease (SCD). However, the precise regulatory mechanisms governing γ-globin repression remain incompletely defined. Here, we report that LYAR (Ly-1 antibody reactive clone, human homologue) and NONO (non-POU domain-containing octamer-binding protein) physically interact and co-occupy the γ-globin promoter to jointly repress its transcription. Knockdown of LYAR significantly reduced the recruitment of NONO to the γ-globin promoter. Notably, co-depletion of LYAR and NONO in K562 and HUDEP-2 cells resulted in additive induction of γ-globin expression that exceeded the effects of individual knockdowns and was comparable to BCL11A depletion, the established master regulator of HbF silencing. item.title: THE UBC8-GID E3 UBIQUITIN LIGASE MODULE IS REQUIRED FOR STRESS RESPONSE IN CANDIDA ALBICANS.
item.author: Zeng Z, Chrustowicz J, Spanos C, Cholewa-Waclaw J, Kelly V, Zhao Y, Scharf DH, Munro CA, Schulman BA, Alpi AF, Makrantoni V.
item.description:
Candida albicans is a leading cause of fungal infections in humans. To survive and proliferate within diverse and dynamic host niches, Candida must rapidly adapt, efficiently acquire essential nutrients, and mount protective stress responses. While cellular stress signalling networks are well described, regulation via the ubiquitin system, including E2-E3 ubiquitylation modules, remains largely unexplored in Candida. Here we investigate the multiprotein Glucose Induced Degradation Deficient (GID) E3 ubiquitin ligase complex and its cognate E2 conjugating enzyme, CaUbc8. Utilizing mass spectrometry-based proteomics, we identified conserved GID subunits, including the previously unannotated CaGid5 homologue. item.title: A case for DNA-membrane interactions in the responses to DNA damage.
item.author: Moriel-Carretero M.
item.description:
Eukaryotic cells harbour two genomes, the nuclear and the mitochondrial ones. Both are subjected to spontaneous and induced DNA damage that threatens biological function. In the nucleus, damage in the DNA is detected, signalled and taken care of by a dedicated, complex network of proteins termed the DNA Damage Response (DDR). In the mitochondria, this first-front DNA damage detection network is less characterized, despite that effective, downstream mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) repair is documented. Also, given that mtDNA exists as multiple copies inside a single mitochondrion, the cell can selectively get rid of unhealthy mtDNA molecules. item.title: Glucocorticoid Receptor Interacts with the TRKB Transmembrane Domain and modulates TRKB Dimerization and Neuronal Plasticity.

item.description:
The overlapping effects on neuronal plasticity of acute increase in glucocorticoid levels and the BDNF-TRKB signaling indicate a deep interconnection between the two pathways. Moreover, chronic stress with elevated glucocorticoids levels and downregulation of TRKB signaling associated with reduced BDNF are both involved in the pathophysiology of different psychiatric disorders. However, the mechanism by which TRKB and glucocorticoid receptors are recruited together in the modulation of neuronal plasticity is not clear yet. In this study we investigated the molecular mechanisms underlying the interplay of glucocorticoids and TRKB signaling in vitro and in vivo.
